The readers differed regarding the recitation of this. Abu al-Duha Muslim ibn Subayh read it: ﴿And when the buried infant girl asked for what sin she was killed﴾, meaning: the buried infant girl asked those who buried her alive: for what sin did they kill her.

Mention of the transmission of this reading:

⁕ Abu al-Sa'ib related to me, saying: Abu Mu'awiyah related to us, from al-Amash, from Muslim, concerning His words: ﴿And when the buried infant girl asked﴾. He said: She demanded retribution for her blood.

⁕ Sawwar ibn Abd Allah al-Anbari related to us, saying: Yahya ibn Said related to us, from al-Amash, who said: Abu al-Duha said, concerning ﴿And when the buried infant girl asked﴾: She asked her killers.

If a reader from among those who read ﴿asalat bi-ayyi dhanbin qutilat﴾ had a basis for it, and the meaning of those who read ﴿bi-ayyi dhanbin qutilat﴾ would have been the same, except that when it is a report of speech, both readings are permissible. This is as one says: "Abd Allah said: For what sin was he struck?" As 'Antarah said:

The two who revile my honour, though I did not revile them, and who vow, when I meet them, to shed my blood.

That is because they used to say: "When we meet 'Antarah, we will surely kill him," so 'Antarah related their speech in his poetry. Likewise is the saying of another:

Two men from Dabbah informed us that we saw a naked man.

The meaning: they informed us that they [had seen]. But the speech follows the manner of reported speech.

Some of the common readers of the metropolitan centres read: ﴿And when the buried infant girl is asked for what sin she was killed﴾, meaning: the buried infant girl was asked for what sin she was killed. The meaning of "qutilat" is: she was killed. However, this was returned to the report in the form of reported speech, like the earlier speech. The meaning of this may also be that it means: "And when the buried infant girl asked her killers and those who buried her alive: For what sin did they kill her?" Then this was referred to what has no named agent, so it was said: "For what sin was she killed."

The more correct of the two readings in our view is the reading of those who read ﴿su'ilat﴾ with a dammah on the sin, ﴿bi-ayyi dhanbin qutilat﴾, in the form of a report, due to the consensus (ijma') of the authoritative readers upon it. The buried infant girl (al-mawudah) is the one buried alive, and so the Arabs used to do to their daughters. From it is the verse of al-Farazdaq ibn Ghalib:

And from us is the one who revived the buried girl, and Amr [or 'Amr], and from us are the bearers and the defenders.

It is said: "He buried her (wa'adaha), so he buries her (ya'iduha), a burial (wa'dan) and a burying (wa'dah)."

Those who gave the interpretation said things similar to what we have said on this.

Mention of those who said this:

⁕ Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Said related to us, from Qatadah: ﴿And when the buried infant girl is asked﴾. In some readings it is: ﴿sa'alat bi-ayyi dhanbin qutilat﴾, not "bi-dhanb." The people of the Jahiliyyah used to kill one of them, their daughter, while they fed their dog, so Allah censured them for that.

⁕ Ibn Abd al-Ala related to us, saying: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Mamar, from Qatadah, who said: Qays ibn Asim al-Tamimi came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "I buried eight daughters in the Jahiliyyah." He said: "Free a slave-camel for each one of them" (fa-a'tiq 'an kulli wahidatin badanah).

⁕ Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Mihran related to us, from Sufyan, from his father, from Abu Ya'la, from Rabi ibn Khuthaym, concerning ﴿And when the buried infant girl is asked for what sin she was killed﴾. He said: The Arabs were among the most inclined of people to do that.

⁕ Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Waki related to us, from Sufyan, from his father, from Abu Ya'la, from Rabi ibn Khaytham, the same.

⁕ Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, concerning His words: ﴿And when the buried infant girl is asked﴾. He said: They are the daughters whom the tribes of the Arabs used to kill, and he recited: "for what sin she was killed."

* *

And His words: ﴿And when the pages are unrolled﴾

Allah, may He be exalted, says: "And when the pages are unfolded" (i.e., the pages of the deeds of the servants are spread open after they had been rolled up, with what was written in them of good deeds and bad deeds).

Those who interpret the Qur'an (ahl al-ta'wil) have said something similar to what we have said regarding this.

Mention of those who said this:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿And when the pages are unfolded﴾: "Your page, O son of Adam, will be read out to you what is in it, then it will be rolled up, then it will be unfolded for you on the Day of Resurrection."

The reciters differed in reading this. The majority of the reciters of Madinah recited ﴿nushirat﴾ with the shin lightened (nushirat, with a single sin), and likewise some of the Kufans recited it. Some of the reciters of Makkah and the majority of the reciters of Kufa recited it with the shin doubled (nushshirat). Those who favoured their reading in this form argued with the saying of Allah: ﴿that He should give him scrolls unfolded (munashshara)﴾, where He did not say munshura. The doubling is appropriate here because it is a report about a plurality, as one says: "These are slaughtered rams" (kibash muddhabbaha); if one reported about a single one, it would be lightened, and one would say "mudhbuha" (slaughtered). Likewise His saying "munshura" [in the singular form of the adjective, applies to the lighter reading].

The interpretation (ta'wil) of His words, exalted is He: ﴿When the sky is stripped away (11), when Hellfire is kindled (12), when Paradise is brought near (13), a soul will know what it has presented (14). So I swear by the receding stars (15), the ones that run and hide (16).﴾

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: "And when the sky is pulled off, drawn away, and then rolled up."

The interpreters (ahl al-ta'wil) said the same as what we have said about this.

Those who said that:

Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us. And al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿kushitat﴾ [stripped away]. He said: "It was pulled away." It is mentioned that in the recitation of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) it was ﴿qushitat﴾ with a qaf. Qasht and kashtu have one meaning, and this is a substitution by the Arabs of the kaf with a qaf because their articulation points are close, as it was said kafur as qafur, and kusṭ as qusṭ. This is common in their speech: when the two letters' points of articulation are close, each one is replaced by the other, as in their saying for the stones of the cooking-pot, athafi as athathi, and thawb farqabi and tharqabi.

* *

His words: ﴿And when Hellfire is kindled﴾

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: "And when Hellfire is set alight and blazed."

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding ﴿and when Hellfire is kindled﴾: "Its kindling is by the wrath of Allah and the sins of the children of Adam."

* *

His words: ﴿So I swear by the receding stars, the ones that run and hide﴾

The interpreters differed regarding al-khunnas al-jawari al-kunnas. Some of them said: they are the five shining planets which recede in their course, then return and hide, concealing themselves in their homes as gazelles hide in caves. The five planets are Bahram (Mars), Zuhal (Saturn), Utarid (Mercury), al-Zuhara (Venus), and al-Mushtari (Jupiter).

Those who said that:

Hannad narrated to us, saying: Abu al-Ahwas narrated to us, from Simak, from Khalid ibn Ururah, that a man stood before Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) and said: "What is ﴿al-jawari al-kunnas﴾?" He said: "They are the planets."

Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, saying: Shu'ba narrated to us, from Simak ibn Harb, who said: I heard Khalid ibn Ururah say: I heard Ali (peace be upon him), when he was asked about ﴿I swear by the receding ones, the ones that run and hide﴾, say: "They are the stars that recede by day and hide by night."

Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from Simak, from Khalid ibn Ururah, from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "The stars."

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Abu Ishaq, from a man of Murad, from Ali, that he said: "Do you know what al-khunas are? They are the stars that run by night and recede by day."

Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Jarir ibn Hazim narrated to me, that he heard al-Hasan being asked. It was said: "O Abu Sa'id, what are al-jawari al-kunnas?" He said: "The stars."

Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Hawdha ibn Khalifa narrated to us, saying: Awf narrated to us, from Bakr ibn Abdullah, regarding His words ﴿So I swear by the receding stars, the ones that run and hide﴾: "They are the shining stars that run facing the east."

Abu al-Sa'ib narrated to me, saying: Abu Mu'awiya narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Mujahid, who said: "They are the stars."

Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Abu Ishaq, from a man of Murad, from Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him), regarding ﴿So I swear by the receding stars, the ones that run and hide﴾: He said: "He means the stars that hide by day and appear by night."

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding His words ﴿So I swear by the receding stars, the ones that run and hide﴾: He said: "They are the stars that appear by night and recede by day."

Ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from al-Hasan regarding His words ﴿So I swear by the receding stars, the ones that run and hide﴾: He said: "They are the stars that recede by day, and al-jawari al-kunnas are their movement when they set."

Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words ﴿I swear by the receding stars, the ones that run and hide﴾: "Al-khunnas and al-jawari al-kunnas are the receding stars. Indeed they recede, lagging behind their rising point; every year they lag behind the earlier time of that rising from which they recede. And al-kunus is that they hide by day so they are not seen. He said: 'And al-jawari run afterward.' So this is al-khunnas, al-jawari, al-kunnas."

Others said: they are the wild cattle that hide in their hiding places.

Those who said that:

al-Hasan ibn Arafa narrated to us, saying: Hushaym ibn Bashir narrated to us, from Zakariyya ibn Abi Za'ida, from Abu Ishaq al-Sabi'i, from Abu Maysara, from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, that he said to Abu Maysara: "What are al-jawari al-kunnas?" He said: "The wild cattle." He said: "I too see that."

Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Yahya narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu Maysara, from Abdullah, regarding His words ﴿al-jawari al-kunnas﴾: He said: "The wild cattle."

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Abu Ishaq, from Amr ibn Shurahbil, who said: Ibn Mas'ud said: "O Amr, what are al-jawari al-kunnas, or what do you think they are?" Amr said: "I think they are cattle." Abdullah said: "I too think they are cattle."

Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu Maysara, who said: "I asked Abdullah about them," and he mentioned something similar.

Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Jarir ibn Hazim narrated to me, saying: al-Hajjaj ibn al-Mundhir narrated to me, saying: I asked Abu al-Sha'tha Jabir ibn Zayd about al-jawari al-kunnas, and he said: "They are cattle when they hide in their hiding places."

Yunus said: Abdullah ibn Wahb said to me: "They are the cattle when they flee from wolves, and that is what he meant by his saying: 'They hid in their hiding places.'"

Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Jarir said, and al-Salt ibn Rashid narrated to me, from Mujahid, the same.

Abu al-Sa'ib narrated to me, saying: Abu Mu'awiya narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Ibrahim, regarding His words ﴿al-jawari al-kunnas﴾: He said: "They are the wild cattle."

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from Mughira, who said: Mujahid was asked while we were with Ibrahim about His words ﴿al-jawari al-kunnas﴾. He said: "I do not know." Ibrahim rebuked him and said: "Why do you not know?" He said: "They narrate from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him)," and we used to hear that they are cattle. Ibrahim said: "They are cattle. Al-jawari al-kunnas are the resting places of wild cattle to which they retreat, and al-khunas al-jawari are the cattle."

Ya'qub narrated to us, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: Mughira informed us, from Ibrahim and Mujahid, that they discussed this verse ﴿So I swear by the receding stars, the ones that run and hide﴾. Ibrahim said to Mujahid: "Say about it what you have heard." Mujahid said: "We used to hear something about it, and some people say they are the stars." Ibrahim said: "They lie about Ali (may Allah be pleased with him). This is like what they narrate from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), that he made the lower part include the upper, and the upper the lower."

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, from al-Mughira, who said: Mujahid was asked about al-jawari al-kunnas and said: "I do not know. They claim they are cattle." Ibrahim said: "What you do not know, they are cattle." He said: "They mention from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) that they are the stars." He said: "They lie about Ali (peace be upon him)."

Others said: they are gazelles.

Those who said that:

Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿So I swear by the receding stars, the ones that run and hide﴾: He meant the gazelles.

Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Ibn Yaman narrated to us, from Ash'ath ibn Ishaq, from Ja'far, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding ﴿So I swear by the receding stars﴾: "The gazelles."

Ya'qub narrated to me, saying: Ibn Ulayya narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Najih narrated to us, from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿So I swear by the receding stars, the ones that run and hide﴾: He said: "We used to say [I think he said]: the gazelles, until Sa'id ibn Jubayr claimed that he asked Ibn Abbas about it, and he repeated its recitation to him."

I was told by al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: Ubayd narrated to us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His words ﴿al-khunas al-jawari al-kunnas﴾: "He means the gazelles."

The most correct of these sayings is that it should be said: Allah, exalted is His remembrance, swore by things that recede at times, meaning they hide, and run at times, and hide at others. Their hiding is that they shelter in their hiding places. Al-makanis (hiding places), in the language of the Arabs, are the places to which wild cattle and gazelles retreat; its singular is maknis and kanas. As al-A'sha said:

When we reached the tribe, a long-necked one with pleasant sound [...]
just as a gazelle stretches its neck beneath the hiding places.

[Diwanuhu: 541; al-Naqa'id: 38. "Taf al-khayal": he came to you by night; al-lamam: a brief meeting. Al-zawr: the visitor; it is said of the singular, dual and plural: zawr. "So return to your visitor" means: return his greeting as he greeted you.]

Here, these are plurals of maknis. And as Tarafa ibn al-Abd said about the kanas:

As if two kanas of a wild cow enclose her,
and the edges of bows beneath a firm backbone.

[In the printed edition: "The meaning: praise be to Allah..."]

As for the proof that kanas may be for gazelles, it is the saying of Aws ibn Hajar:

Did you not see that Allah sent down rain,
and the fawn gazelles in the kanas were sheltering?

[Thus Abu Ja'far (may Allah have mercy on him) went to the view that "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate" is not a verse of al-Fatiha, and he argued for his view with what you see. This is not the place to expand on that disagreement, and the evidence against what Ibn Jarir said is well known.

I have investigated this question and set out, in my judgment and understanding, the sound proofs that it is a verse of al-Fatiha, in my commentary on Sunan al-Tirmidhi, 2:16–25, and an allusion to it here suffices. Ahmad Muhammad Shakir.]

So kanas, in the language of the Arabs, is as I have described, and it is not objectionable that this term be borrowed for the places in the sky where the stars are. Since this is so, and there is no indication in the verse that what is meant by it is the stars rather than the wild cattle, nor the wild cattle rather than the gazelles, the correct view is that it covers everything whose attribute is receding at times and running at others, and hiding at intervals, according to what His majesty and praise described as their attribute.

Some of them said: they are the five shining planets which recede in their course, then return and hide, concealing themselves in their homes as gazelles hide in caves. The five planets are Bahram (Mars), Zuhal (Saturn), Utarid (Mercury), al-Zuhara (Venus), and al-Mushtari (Jupiter).

Those who said that:

Hannad narrated to us, saying: Abu al-Ahwas narrated to us, from Simak, from Khalid ibn Ururah, that a man stood before Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) and said: "What is ﴿al-jawari al-kunnas﴾?" He said: "They are the planets."

Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, saying: Shu'ba narrated to us, from Simak ibn Harb, who said: I heard Khalid ibn Ururah say: I heard Ali (peace be upon him), when he was asked about ﴿I swear by the receding ones, the ones that run and hide﴾, say: "They are the stars that recede by day and hide by night."

Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from Simak, from Khalid ibn Ururah, from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "The stars."

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Abu Ishaq, from a man of Murad, from Ali, that he said: "Do you know what al-khunas are? They are the stars that run by night and recede by day."

Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Jarir ibn Hazim narrated to me, that he heard al-Hasan being asked. It was said: "O Abu Sa'id, what are al-jawari al-kunnas?" He said: "The stars."

Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Hawdha ibn Khalifa narrated to us, saying: Awf narrated to us, from Bakr ibn Abdullah, regarding His words ﴿So I swear by the receding stars, the ones that run and hide﴾: "They are the shining stars that run facing the east."

Abu al-Sa'ib narrated to me, saying: Abu Mu'awiya narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Mujahid, who said: "They are the stars."

Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Abu Ishaq, from a man of Murad, from Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him), regarding ﴿So I swear by the receding stars, the ones that run and hide﴾: He said: "He means the stars that hide by day and appear by night."

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding His words ﴿So I swear by the receding stars, the ones that run and hide﴾: He said: "They are the stars that appear by night and recede by day."

Ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from al-Hasan regarding His words ﴿So I swear by the receding stars, the ones that run and hide﴾: He said: "They are the stars that recede by day, and al-jawari al-kunnas are their movement when they set."

Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words ﴿I swear by the receding stars, the ones that run and hide﴾: "Al-khunnas and al-jawari al-kunnas are the receding stars. Indeed they recede, lagging behind their rising point; every year they lag behind the earlier time of that rising from which they recede. And al-kunus is that they hide by day so they are not seen. He said: 'And al-jawari run afterward.' So this is al-khunnas, al-jawari, al-kunnas."

Others said: they are the wild cattle that hide in their hiding places.

Those who said that:

al-Hasan ibn Arafa narrated to us, saying: Hushaym ibn Bashir narrated to us, from Zakariyya ibn Abi Za'ida, from Abu Ishaq al-Sabi'i, from Abu Maysara, from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, that he said to Abu Maysara: "What are al-jawari al-kunnas?" He said: "The wild cattle." He said: "I too see that."

Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Yahya narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu Maysara, from Abdullah, regarding His words ﴿al-jawari al-kunnas﴾: He said: "The wild cattle."

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Abu Ishaq, from Amr ibn Shurahbil, who said: Ibn Mas'ud said: "O Amr, what are al-jawari al-kunnas, or what do you think they are?" Amr said: "I think they are cattle." Abdullah said: "I too think they are cattle."

Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu Maysara, who said: "I asked Abdullah about them," and he mentioned something similar.

Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Jarir ibn Hazim narrated to me, saying: al-Hajjaj ibn al-Mundhir narrated to me, saying: I asked Abu al-Sha'tha Jabir ibn Zayd about al-jawari al-kunnas, and he said: "They are cattle when they hide in their hiding places."

Yunus said: Abdullah ibn Wahb said to me: "They are the cattle when they flee from wolves, and that is what he meant by his saying: 'They hid in their hiding places.'"

Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Jarir said, and al-Salt ibn Rashid narrated to me, from Mujahid, the same.

Abu al-Sa'ib narrated to me, saying: Abu Mu'awiya narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Ibrahim, regarding His words ﴿al-jawari al-kunnas﴾: He said: "They are the wild cattle."

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from Mughira, who said: Mujahid was asked while we were with Ibrahim about His words ﴿al-jawari al-kunnas﴾. He said: "I do not know." Ibrahim rebuked him and said: "Why do you not know?" He said: "They narrate from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him)," and we used to hear that they are cattle. Ibrahim said: "They are cattle. Al-jawari al-kunnas are the resting places of wild cattle to which they retreat, and al-khunas al-jawari are the cattle."

Ya'qub narrated to us, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: Mughira informed us, from Ibrahim and Mujahid, that they discussed this verse ﴿So I swear by the receding stars, the ones that run and hide﴾. Ibrahim said to Mujahid: "Say about it what you have heard." Mujahid said: "We used to hear something about it, and some people say they are the stars." Ibrahim said: "They lie about Ali (may Allah be pleased with him). This is like what they narrate from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), that he made the lower part include the upper, and the upper the lower."

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, from al-Mughira, who said: Mujahid was asked about al-jawari al-kunnas and said: "I do not know. They claim they are cattle." Ibrahim said: "What you do not know, they are cattle." He said: "They mention from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) that they are the stars." He said: "They lie about Ali (peace be upon him)."

Others said: they are gazelles.

Those who said that:

Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿So I swear by the receding stars, the ones that run and hide﴾: He meant the gazelles.

Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Ibn Yaman narrated to us, from Ash'ath ibn Ishaq, from Ja'far, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding ﴿So I swear by the receding stars﴾: "The gazelles."

Ya'qub narrated to me, saying: Ibn Ulayya narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Najih narrated to us, from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿So I swear by the receding stars, the ones that run and hide﴾: He said: "We used to say [I think he said]: the gazelles, until Sa'id ibn Jubayr claimed that he asked Ibn Abbas about it, and he repeated its recitation to him."

I was told by al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: Ubayd narrated to us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His words ﴿al-khunas al-jawari al-kunnas﴾: "He means the gazelles."

The most correct of these sayings is that it should be said: Allah, exalted is His remembrance, swore by things that recede at times, meaning they hide, and run at times, and hide at others. Their hiding is that they shelter in their hiding places. Al-makanis (hiding places), in the language of the Arabs, are the places to which wild cattle and gazelles retreat; its singular is maknis and kanas. As al-A'sha said:

When we reached the tribe, a long-necked one with pleasant sound [...]
just as a gazelle stretches its neck beneath the hiding places.

[Diwanuhu: 541; al-Naqa'id: 38. "Taf al-khayal": he came to you by night; al-lamam: a brief meeting. Al-zawr: the visitor; it is said of the singular, dual and plural: zawr. "So return to your visitor" means: return his greeting as he greeted you.]

Here, these are plurals of maknis. And as Tarafa ibn al-Abd said about the kanas:

As if two kanas of a wild cow enclose her,
and the edges of bows beneath a firm backbone.

[In the printed edition: "The meaning: praise be to Allah..."]

As for the proof that kanas may be for gazelles, it is the saying of Aws ibn Hajar:

Did you not see that Allah sent down rain,
and the fawn gazelles in the kanas were sheltering?

[Thus Abu Ja'far (may Allah have mercy on him) went to the view that "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate" is not a verse of al-Fatiha, and he argued for his view with what you see. This is not the place to expand on that disagreement, and the evidence against what Ibn Jarir said is well known.

So kanas, in the language of the Arabs, is as I have described, and it is not objectionable that this term be borrowed for the places in the sky where the stars are. The interpretation (ta'wil) of His words, exalted is He: ﴿When the sky is stripped away (11), when Hellfire is kindled (12), when Paradise is brought near (13), a soul will know what it has presented (14). So I swear by the receding stars (15), the ones that run and hide (16).﴾

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: "And when the sky is pulled off, drawn away, and then rolled up."

The interpreters (ahl al-ta'wil) said the same as what we have said about this.

Those who said that:

Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us. And al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿kushitat﴾ [stripped away]. This is common in their speech: when the two letters' points of articulation are close, each one is replaced by the other, as in their saying for the stones of the cooking-pot, athafi as athathi, and thawb farqabi and tharqabi.

* *

His words: ﴿And when Hellfire is kindled﴾

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: "And when Hellfire is set alight and blazed."

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding ﴿and when Hellfire is kindled﴾: "Its kindling is by the wrath of Allah and the sins of the children of Adam."

The reciters differed in reading it. The common reciters of Madina read ﴿su"-"-irat﴾ with the ayn doubled, meaning it was lit again and again, while the common reciters of Kufa read it with the lightened form. The position on this is that both are well-known recitations, and whichever one the reader recites is correct.

* *

His words: ﴿And when Paradise is brought near﴾

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: "And when Paradise is brought near and drawn close."

The interpreters said the same as what we have said about this.

Those who said that:

Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from Sufyan, from his father, from Abu Ya'la, from al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym, regarding ﴿And when Hellfire is kindled and when Paradise is brought near﴾: "To these two the discourse proceeded: a group in Paradise and a group in the blaze."

Ibn Humayd narrated to me, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, from his father, from Abu Ya'la, from al-Rabi': ﴿And when Hellfire is kindled and when Paradise is brought near﴾ He said: "To these two the discourse proceeded: a group to Paradise and a group to the Fire." By al-Rabi's saying "to these two the discourse proceeded," he meant that the beginning of the report, ﴿When the sun is folded up...﴾ up to His words ﴿and when Hellfire is kindled﴾, enumerates the events that will occur, whose end is one of these two matters, and that destination is either to Paradise or to the Fire.

* *

His words: ﴿A soul will know what it has presented﴾

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: "At that time a soul will know what it has presented of good, by which it arrives at Paradise, or of evil, by which it arrives at the Fire." He means: at that moment there will become clear to it what it was ignorant of, and what was its well-being from other things.

The interpreters said the same as what we have said about this.

Those who said that:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding ﴿a soul will know what it has presented﴾ [of deeds], he said: Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "To this the discourse proceeded."

* *

His words: ﴿A soul will know what it has presented﴾

This is the answer (jawab) to His words ﴿When the sun is folded up﴾ and what follows it, as one says: "When Abdullah stands up, Amr sits down."

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: "And when Paradise is brought near and drawn close."

The interpreters said the same as what we have said about this.

Those who said that:

Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from Sufyan, from his father, from Abu Ya'la, from al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym, regarding ﴿And when Hellfire is kindled and when Paradise is brought near﴾: "To these two the discourse proceeded: a group in Paradise and a group in the blaze."

Ibn Humayd narrated to me, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, from his father, from Abu Ya'la, from al-Rabi': ﴿And when Hellfire is kindled and when Paradise is brought near﴾ He said: "To these two the discourse proceeded: a group to Paradise and a group to the Fire." By al-Rabi's saying "to these two the discourse proceeded," he meant that the beginning of the report, ﴿When the sun is folded up...﴾ up to His words ﴿and when Hellfire is kindled﴾, enumerates the events that will occur, whose end is one of these two matters, and that destination is either to Paradise or to the Fire.

* *

His words: ﴿A soul will know what it has presented﴾

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: "At that time a soul will know what it has presented of good, by which it arrives at Paradise, or of evil, by which it arrives at the Fire." He means: at that moment there will become clear to it what it was ignorant of, and what was its well-being from other things.

The interpreters said the same as what we have said about this.

Those who said that:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding ﴿a soul will know what it has presented﴾ [of deeds], he said: Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "To this the discourse proceeded."

* *

His words: ﴿A soul will know what it has presented﴾

This is the answer (jawab) to His words ﴿When the sun is folded up﴾ and what follows it, as one says: "When Abdullah stands up, Amr sits down."

* *

His words: ﴿So I swear by the receding stars, the ones that run and hide﴾

The interpreters differed regarding al-khunnas al-jawari al-kunnas. Some of them said: they are the five shining planets which recede in their course, then return and hide, concealing themselves in their homes as gazelles hide in caves. The five planets are Bahram (Mars), Zuhal (Saturn), Utarid (Mercury), al-Zuhara (Venus), and al-Mushtari (Jupiter).

Those who said that:

Hannad narrated to us, saying: Abu al-Ahwas narrated to us, from Simak, from Khalid ibn Ururah, that a man stood before Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) and said: "What is ﴿al-jawari al-kunnas﴾?" He said: "They are the planets."

Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, saying: Shu'ba narrated to us, from Simak ibn Harb, who said: I heard Khalid ibn Ururah say: I heard Ali (peace be upon him), when he was asked about ﴿I swear by the receding ones, the ones that run and hide﴾, say: "They are the stars that recede by day and hide by night."

Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from Simak, from Khalid ibn Ururah, from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "The stars."

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Abu Ishaq, from a man of Murad, from Ali, that he said: "Do you know what al-khunas are? They are the stars that run by night and recede by day."

Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Jarir ibn Hazim narrated to me, that he heard al-Hasan being asked. It was said: "O Abu Sa'id, what are al-jawari al-kunnas?" He said: "The stars."

Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Hawdha ibn Khalifa narrated to us, saying: Awf narrated to us, from Bakr ibn Abdullah, regarding His words ﴿So I swear by the receding stars, the ones that run and hide﴾: "They are the shining stars that run facing the east."

Abu al-Sa'ib narrated to me, saying: Abu Mu'awiya narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Mujahid, who said: "They are the stars."

Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Abu Ishaq, from a man of Murad, from Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him), regarding ﴿So I swear by the receding stars, the ones that run and hide﴾: He said: "He means the stars that hide by day and appear by night."

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding His words ﴿So I swear by the receding stars, the ones that run and hide﴾: He said: "They are the stars that appear by night and recede by day."

Ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from al-Hasan regarding His words ﴿So I swear by the receding stars, the ones that run and hide﴾: He said: "They are the stars that recede by day, and al-jawari al-kunnas are their movement when they set."

Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words ﴿I swear by the receding stars, the ones that run and hide﴾: "Al-khunnas and al-jawari al-kunnas are the receding stars. Indeed they recede, lagging behind their rising point; every year they lag behind the earlier time of that rising from which they recede. And al-kunus is that they hide by day so they are not seen. He said: 'And al-jawari run afterward.' So this is al-khunnas, al-jawari, al-kunnas."

Others said: they are the wild cattle that hide in their hiding places.

Those who said that:

al-Hasan ibn Arafa narrated to us, saying: Hushaym ibn Bashir narrated to us, from Zakariyya ibn Abi Za'ida, from Abu Ishaq al-Sabi'i, from Abu Maysara, from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, that he said to Abu Maysara: "What are al-jawari al-kunnas?" He said: "The wild cattle." He said: "I too see that."

Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Yahya narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu Maysara, from Abdullah, regarding His words ﴿al-jawari al-kunnas﴾: He said: "The wild cattle."

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Abu Ishaq, from Amr ibn Shurahbil, who said: Ibn Mas'ud said: "O Amr, what are al-jawari al-kunnas, or what do you think they are?" Amr said: "I think they are cattle." Abdullah said: "I too think they are cattle."

Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu Maysara, who said: "I asked Abdullah about them," and he mentioned something similar.

Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Jarir ibn Hazim narrated to me, saying: al-Hajjaj ibn al-Mundhir narrated to me, saying: I asked Abu al-Sha'tha Jabir ibn Zayd about al-jawari al-kunnas, and he said: "They are cattle when they hide in their hiding places."

Yunus said: Abdullah ibn Wahb said to me: "They are the cattle when they flee from wolves, and that is what he meant by his saying: 'They hid in their hiding places.'"

Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Jarir said, and al-Salt ibn Rashid narrated to me, from Mujahid, the same.

Abu al-Sa'ib narrated to me, saying: Abu Mu'awiya narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Ibrahim, regarding His words ﴿al-jawari al-kunnas﴾: He said: "They are the wild cattle."

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from Mughira, who said: Mujahid was asked while we were with Ibrahim about His words ﴿al-jawari al-kunnas﴾. He said: "I do not know." Ibrahim rebuked him and said: "Why do you not know?" He said: "They narrate from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him)," and we used to hear that they are cattle. Ibrahim said: "They are cattle. Al-jawari al-kunnas are the resting places of wild cattle to which they retreat, and al-khunas al-jawari are the cattle."

Ya'qub narrated to us, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: Mughira informed us, from Ibrahim and Mujahid, that they discussed this verse ﴿So I swear by the receding stars, the ones that run and hide﴾. Ibrahim said to Mujahid: "Say about it what you have heard." Mujahid said: "We used to hear something about it, and some people say they are the stars." Ibrahim said: "They lie about Ali (may Allah be pleased with him). This is like what they narrate from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), that he made the lower part include the upper, and the upper the lower."

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, from al-Mughira, who said: Mujahid was asked about al-jawari al-kunnas and said: "I do not know. They claim they are cattle." Ibrahim said: "What you do not know, they are cattle." He said: "They mention from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) that they are the stars." He said: "They lie about Ali (peace be upon him)."

Others said: they are gazelles.

Those who said that:

Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿So I swear by the receding stars, the ones that run and hide﴾: He meant the gazelles.

Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Ibn Yaman narrated to us, from Ash'ath ibn Ishaq, from Ja'far, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding ﴿So I swear by the receding stars﴾: "The gazelles."

Ya'qub narrated to me, saying: Ibn Ulayya narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Najih narrated to us, from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿So I swear by the receding stars, the ones that run and hide﴾: He said: "We used to say [I think he said]: the gazelles, until Sa'id ibn Jubayr claimed that he asked Ibn Abbas about it, and he repeated its recitation to him."

I was told by al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: Ubayd narrated to us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His words ﴿al-khunas al-jawari al-kunnas﴾: "He means the gazelles."

The most correct of these sayings is that it should be said: Allah, exalted is His remembrance, swore by things that recede at times, meaning they hide, and run at times, and hide at others. Their hiding is that they shelter in their hiding places. Al-makanis (hiding places), in the language of the Arabs, are the places to which wild cattle and gazelles retreat; its singular is maknis and kanas. As al-A'sha said:

When we reached the tribe, a long-necked one with pleasant sound [...]
just as a gazelle stretches its neck beneath the hiding places.

[Diwanuhu: 541; al-Naqa'id: 38. "Taf al-khayal": he came to you by night; al-lamam: a brief meeting. Al-zawr: the visitor; it is said of the singular, dual and plural: zawr. "So return to your visitor" means: return his greeting as he greeted you.]

Here, these are plurals of maknis. And as Tarafa ibn al-Abd said about the kanas:

As if two kanas of a wild cow enclose her,
and the edges of bows beneath a firm backbone.

[In the printed edition: "The meaning: praise be to Allah..."]

As for the proof that kanas may be for gazelles, it is the saying of Aws ibn Hajar:

Did you not see that Allah sent down rain,
and the fawn gazelles in the kanas were sheltering?

[Thus Abu Ja'far (may Allah have mercy on him) went to the view that "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate" is not a verse of al-Fatiha, and he argued for his view with what you see. This is not the place to expand on that disagreement, and the evidence against what Ibn Jarir said is well known.

I have investigated this question and set out, in my judgment and understanding, the sound proofs that it is a verse of al-Fatiha, in my commentary on Sunan al-Tirmidhi, 2:16–25, and an allusion to it here suffices. Ahmad Muhammad Shakir.]

So kanas, in the language of the Arabs, is as I have described, and it is not objectionable that this term be borrowed for the places in the sky where the stars are. Since this is so, and there is no indication in the verse that what is meant by it is the stars rather than the wild cattle, nor the wild cattle rather than the gazelles, the correct view is that it covers everything whose attribute is receding at times and running at others, and hiding at intervals, according to what His majesty and praise described as their attribute.

On the words of God, the Exalted: ﴿By the night when it turns its back﴾ (17) ﴿and by the morning when it breathes﴾ (18) ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger﴾ (19) ﴿possessing power, with esteem near the Lord of the Throne﴾ (20).

Our Lord, may His praise be exalted, swears by the night when it 'as'asa (turns its back), meaning: and He swears by the night when it 'as'asa.

The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) differed regarding His words ﴿and by the night when it 'as'asa﴾. Some of them said: by His words ﴿when it 'as'asa﴾ is meant: when it turns its back (adbara).

Those who said this:

* Ali related to me, saying: Abu Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiya related to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿and by the night when it 'as'asa﴾, he said: "when it turns its back."

* Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my paternal uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿and by the night when it 'as'asa﴾, he meant: "when it turns its back."

* Abd al-Hamid ibn Bayan al-Yashkuri related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Yazid related to us, from Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid, from a man, from Abu Zabyan, who said: I was following Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him), and he was going out toward the east, and he met the dawn, and he recited this verse: ﴿and by the night when it 'as'asa﴾.

* Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Ibn Idris related to us, from al-Hasan ibn Ubayd Allah, from Sa'd ibn Ubayda, from Abu Abd al-Rahman, who said: Ali (peace be upon him) came out from the side of the market gate, when the dawn had risen or the daybreak, and he recited: ﴿and by the night when it 'as'asa and by the morning when it breathes﴾, then said: "Where is the one who asked about the witr? Yes, this is the hour of the witr."

Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu Asim related to us, saying: Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa related to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid regarding His words ﴿and by the night when it 'as'asa﴾, he said: "its approach," and it is also said: "its turning away."

* Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatada, regarding His words ﴿and by the night when it 'as'asa﴾: "when it turns its back."

* Ibn Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatada, ﴿when it 'as'asa﴾, he said: "when it turns its back."

* It was narrated to me from al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: Ubayd related to us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His words ﴿when it 'as'asa﴾: "when it turns its back."

* Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Waki' related to us, from Mis'ar, from Abu Husayn, from Abu Abd al-Rahman, who said: Ali (peace be upon him) came out after the muezzin had called the dawn call, and said: ﴿and by the night when it 'as'asa and by the morning when it breathes﴾ "Where is the one who asked about the witr?" He said: "Yes, this is the hour of the witr."

* Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words ﴿and by the night when it 'as'asa﴾: "'as'asa means turned away (tawalla)," and he said: "the dawn breathes from here," pointing toward the east, the rising of the dawn.

Others said: by His words ﴿when it 'as'asa﴾ is meant: when it approaches with its darkness.

Those who said this:

* Ibn Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from al-Hasan, ﴿and by the night when it 'as'asa﴾, he said: "when it covers the people."

* al-Husayn ibn Ali al-Sada'i related to us, saying: my father related to me, from al-Fudayl, from Atiyya, (and by the night when it 'as'asa), he said: "He pointed with his hand toward the west."

The more correct of the two interpretations in my view is the saying of the one who said: the meaning is "when it turns its back," because of His words ﴿and by the morning when it breathes﴾, which indicates that the oath is by the night turning away and by the day approaching. The Arabs say: "'as'asa al-layl" and "sa'sa'a al-layl" when it turns its back and only a little of it remains. Among that is the verse of Ru'ba ibn al-Ajjaj:

Ya Hind, how quickly it has sa'sa'a,
and if it could, it would follow the tail of the breeze.

This is the dialect of those who say "sa'sa'a." As for the dialect of those who say "'as'asa," it is the verse of Alqama ibn Qurt:

Until, when the dawn has breathed for it,
and its night has been stripped away and 'as'asa.

That is, it turned its back. Some scholars of Arabic speech claimed that 'as'asa means it drew near its beginning and grew dark. Al-Farra' said: Abu al-Bilad the grammarian used to recite a line:

'As'asa, until if it wished it would draw near,
there would be for it from its light a torch.

He says: "if it wished, as it drew near," but he assimilated the dhal into the dal. Al-Farra' said: they used to regard this line as fabricated.

He says: the light of the day when it approaches and becomes clear.

The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) differed regarding His words ﴿and by the night when it 'as'asa﴾. Some of them said: by His words ﴿when it 'as'asa﴾ is meant: when it turns its back (adbara).

Those who said this:

* Ali related to me, saying: Abu Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiya related to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿and by the night when it 'as'asa﴾, he said: "when it turns its back."

* Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my paternal uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿and by the night when it 'as'asa﴾, he meant: "when it turns its back."

* Abd al-Hamid ibn Bayan al-Yashkuri related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Yazid related to us, from Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid, from a man, from Abu Zabyan, who said: I was following Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him), and he was going out toward the east, and he met the dawn, and he recited this verse: ﴿and by the night when it 'as'asa﴾.

* Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Ibn Idris related to us, from al-Hasan ibn Ubayd Allah, from Sa'd ibn Ubayda, from Abu Abd al-Rahman, who said: Ali (peace be upon him) came out from the side of the market gate, when the dawn had risen or the daybreak, and he recited: ﴿and by the night when it 'as'asa and by the morning when it breathes﴾, then said: "Where is the one who asked about the witr? Yes, this is the hour of the witr."

Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu Asim related to us, saying: Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa related to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid regarding His words ﴿and by the night when it 'as'asa﴾, he said: "its approach," and it is also said: "its turning away."

* Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatada, regarding His words ﴿and by the night when it 'as'asa﴾: "when it turns its back."

* Ibn Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatada, ﴿when it 'as'asa﴾, he said: "when it turns its back."

* It was narrated to me from al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: Ubayd related to us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His words ﴿when it 'as'asa﴾: "when it turns its back."

* Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Waki' related to us, from Mis'ar, from Abu Husayn, from Abu Abd al-Rahman, who said: Ali (peace be upon him) came out after the muezzin had called the dawn call, and said: ﴿and by the night when it 'as'asa and by the morning when it breathes﴾ "Where is the one who asked about the witr?" He said: "Yes, this is the hour of the witr."

* Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words ﴿and by the night when it 'as'asa﴾: "'as'asa means turned away (tawalla)," and he said: "the dawn breathes from here," pointing toward the east, the rising of the dawn.

Others said: by His words ﴿when it 'as'asa﴾ is meant: when it approaches with its darkness.

Those who said this:

* Ibn Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from al-Hasan, ﴿and by the night when it 'as'asa﴾, he said: "when it covers the people."

* al-Husayn ibn Ali al-Sada'i related to us, saying: my father related to me, from al-Fudayl, from Atiyya, (and by the night when it 'as'asa), he said: "He pointed with his hand toward the west."

The more correct of the two interpretations in my view is the saying of the one who said: the meaning is "when it turns its back," because of His words ﴿and by the morning when it breathes﴾, which indicates that the oath is by the night turning away and by the day approaching. The Arabs say: "'as'asa al-layl" and "sa'sa'a al-layl" when it turns its back and only a little of it remains. Among that is the verse of Ru'ba ibn al-Ajjaj:

Ya Hind, how quickly it has sa'sa'a,
and if it could, it would follow the tail of the breeze.

This is the dialect of those who say "sa'sa'a." As for the dialect of those who say "'as'asa," it is the verse of Alqama ibn Qurt:

Until, when the dawn has breathed for it,
and its night has been stripped away and 'as'asa.

That is, it turned its back. Some scholars of Arabic speech claimed that 'as'asa means it drew near its beginning and grew dark. Al-Farra' said: Abu al-Bilad the grammarian used to recite a line:

'As'asa, until if it wished it would draw near,
there would be for it from its light a torch.

He says: "if it wished, as it drew near," but he assimilated the dhal into the dal. Al-Farra' said: they used to regard this line as fabricated.

* *

And His words ﴿and by the morning when it breathes﴾

He says: the light of the day when it approaches and becomes clear.

The people of interpretation said the same as what we have said.

Those who said this:

* Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Ibn Yaman related to us, from Ash'ath, from Ja'far, from Sa'id, regarding His words ﴿and by the morning when it breathes﴾, he said: "when it arises."

* Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatada, ﴿and by the morning when it breathes﴾: "when it shines and approaches."

* *

And His words ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: indeed this Qur'an is the revelation of a noble messenger, meaning Gabriel, who sent it down upon Muhammad ibn Abd Allah.

The people of interpretation said the same as what we have said.

On the interpretation of His words, ﴿Obeyed there, and trustworthy﴾ (81:21)

God, may His remembrance be exalted, says: ﴿Obeyed there﴾ means Gabriel (ﷺ), obeyed in the heavens, whom the angels obey. ﴿Trustworthy﴾ means: trustworthy with God regarding His revelation and His message, and everything else He has entrusted to him.

Those who interpret the Qur'an (ahl al-ta'wil) have said the same as what we have said.

Mention of those who said that:

- Abu al-Sa'ib related to me, saying: 'Umar ibn Shabib al-Muslili narrated to us, from Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid, from Abu Salih: ﴿Obeyed there, trustworthy﴾ – he said: Gabriel, peace be upon him, trustworthy to enter seventy veils of light without permission.

- Muhammad ibn Mansur al-Tusi narrated to us, saying: 'Umar ibn Shabib narrated to us, saying: Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid narrated to us, saying: I do not know it except from Abu Salih, the like of it.

- Sulayman ibn 'Umar ibn Khalid al-Aqta' narrated to us, saying: my father 'Umar ibn Khalid related to me, from Ma'qil ibn 'Ubayd Allah al-Jazari, who said: Maymun ibn Mihran said regarding His words, ﴿Obeyed there, trustworthy﴾: That is Gabriel, peace be upon him.

- Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my paternal uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words, ﴿Possessor of power, with the Lord of the Throne secure, obeyed there, trustworthy﴾: He said: meaning Gabriel.

- Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah regarding His words, ﴿Possessor of power, with the Lord of the Throne secure, obeyed﴾: obeyed with God, ﴿there, trustworthy﴾.

- I was told, from al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd narrated to us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His words, ﴿Obeyed there, trustworthy﴾: meaning Gabriel, peace be upon him.

* *

And His words: ﴿And your companion is not mad﴾

God, may His remembrance be exalted, says: Your companion, O people, Muhammad, is not mad, so as to speak of a jinn and rave with the raving of madmen, ﴿but he brought the truth and confirmed the messengers﴾.

Those who interpret the Qur'an have said the same as what we have said.

Mention of those who said that:

- Sulayman ibn 'Amr ibn Khalid al-Barqi narrated to us, saying: my father 'Amr ibn Khalid narrated to us, from Ma'qil ibn 'Abd Allah al-Jazari, who said: Maymun ibn Mihran said: ﴿And your companion is not mad﴾: That is Muhammad (ﷺ).

* *

And His words: ﴿And he certainly saw him on the clear horizon﴾

God, may His remembrance be exalted, says: He certainly saw him, that is Muhammad saw Gabriel (ﷺ) in his form, in the direction that makes things clear, so that one sees from it; and that is the direction of the rising of the sun from the east.

Those who interpret the Qur'an have said the same as what we have said.

Mention of those who said that:

- Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid regarding His words, ﴿on the clear horizon﴾: the highest. He said: on the horizon from the direction of Ajyad.

- Ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, ﴿on the clear horizon﴾: He said: We used to be told that the horizon is where the sun rises.

- Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words, ﴿And he certainly saw him on the clear horizon﴾: We used to be told that it is the horizon from which the day comes.

- Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words, ﴿And he certainly saw him on the clear horizon﴾: He saw Gabriel on the clear horizon.

- 'Isa ibn 'Uthman ibn 'Isa al-Ramli related to me, saying: Yahya ibn 'Isa narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from al-Walid ibn al-'Izar, who said: I heard Abu al-Ahwas say regarding God's words, ﴿And he certainly saw him on the clear horizon﴾: He saw Gabriel, who had six hundred wings, in his form.

- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from 'Ata', from 'Amir, who said: Gabriel did not see the Prophet (ﷺ) in his form except once. He used to come to him in the form of a man called Dihya. So he came to him on the day he saw him in his form, having filled the whole horizon, wearing green silk brocade, hung with pearls. That is God's words: ﴿And he certainly saw him on the clear horizon﴾. And it is mentioned that this verse, in "When the sun is folded up" (81:1), ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger﴾ refers to Gabriel, up to His words ﴿and he is not niggardly regarding the unseen﴾, which means the Prophet (ﷺ).

* *

And His words: ﴿And he is not niggardly regarding the unseen﴾

The readers differed in their recitation of this. The majority of the readers of Medina and Kufa recited it ﴿bi-ḍanīn﴾ with the letter ḍād, meaning that he is not stingy towards them in teaching them what God taught him and sent down to him of His Book. Some of the Meccan readers, some of the Basran readers and some of the Kufan readers recited it ﴿bi-ẓanīn﴾ with the letter ẓā', meaning that he is not accused regarding what he informs them of from God's tidings.

Mention of those who recited it with ḍād and interpreted it in the way we have described, from among those who interpret the Qur'an: Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from 'Asim, from Zirr, ﴿and he is not ẓanīn regarding the unseen﴾. He said: al-ẓanīn: the accused. In your recitation: ﴿ḍanīn﴾, and ḍanīn: the stingy; and the unseen: the Qur'an.

- Bishr narrated to us, saying: Khalid ibn 'Abd Allah al-Wasiti narrated to us, saying: al-Mughira narrated to us, from Ibrahim, ﴿and he is not niggardly regarding the unseen﴾: not stingy.

- Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words, ﴿and he is not niggardly regarding the unseen﴾: He said: he does not withhold from you what he knows.

- Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words, ﴿and he is not niggardly regarding the unseen﴾: He said: Indeed this Qur'an is unseen; God gave it to Muhammad, and he disseminated it, taught it and called to it. By God, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) did not withhold it.

- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, from 'Asim, from Zirr, ﴿and he is not ẓanīn regarding the unseen﴾: He said: in our recitation, "accused". And whoever recites ﴿ḍanīn﴾ says: "stingy".

- Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, ﴿and he is not niggardly regarding the unseen﴾: He said: stingy.

- Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words, ﴿and he is not niggardly regarding the unseen﴾: The unseen is the Qur'an. He did not withhold it from anyone among mankind; he delivered and conveyed it. God sent it with the Trustworthy Spirit, Gabriel, to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Gabriel conveyed to Muhammad what God had entrusted to him, and Muhammad conveyed to the servants what God and Gabriel had entrusted to him. None of them was stingy, concealed or spoke conjecturally.

- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from 'Ata', from 'Amir, regarding His words, ﴿and he is not niggardly regarding the unseen﴾: meaning the Prophet (ﷺ).

Mention of those who recited it with ẓā' and interpreted it as we have mentioned, from among those who interpret the Qur'an.

- Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: al-Muharibi narrated to us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, that he recited: ﴿bi-ẓanīn﴾ and said: not accused.

- Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, saying: Shu'ba narrated to us, from Abu al-Mu'alla, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that he used to recite this letter ﴿and he is not ẓanīn regarding the unseen﴾. I said to Sa'id ibn Jubayr: What is al-ẓanīn? He said: not accused.

- Ya'qub related to me, saying: Ibn 'Ulayya narrated to us, from Abu al-Mu'alla, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that he recited: ﴿and he is not ẓanīn regarding the unseen﴾. I said: And what is al-ẓanīn? He said: the accused.

- Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my paternal uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words, ﴿and he is not ẓanīn regarding the unseen﴾: He says: not accused regarding what he has been given, and he is not suspected regarding what he has been given.

- Bishr narrated to us, saying: Khalid ibn 'Abd Allah al-Wasiti narrated to us, saying: al-Mughira narrated to us, from Ibrahim, ﴿and he is not ẓanīn regarding the unseen﴾: He said: accused.

- Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from Sufyan, from 'Asim, from Zirr, ﴿and he is not ẓanīn regarding the unseen﴾: He said: the unseen is the Qur'an. In our recitation, ﴿ẓanīn﴾: accused.

- I was told, from al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd narrated to us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His words, ﴿ẓanīn﴾: He said: not accused regarding what God has sent down.

Some of the scholars of Arabic have interpreted it to mean: and he is not weak regarding the unseen, but he is capable of bearing it and able to manage it; and its basis is the Arabs' saying of a weak man: "huwa ẓanūn" (he is weak).

The more correct of the two recitations in my view is that which the copies of the Muslims' codices agree upon, even though their recitations differ concerning it. That is ﴿ḍanīn﴾ with ḍād, because that is how it is written in all of their copies. Since that is so, the more correct of the two interpretations is the interpretation of the one who interpreted it as: Muhammad, regarding what God taught him of His revelation and His sending down, is not stingy in teaching it to you, O people, but rather he is eager that you believe in it and learn it.

* *

And His words: ﴿And it is not the word of an accursed devil﴾

God, may His remembrance be exalted, says: This Qur'an is not the word of a cursed, expelled devil, but rather it is the speech and revelation of God.

* *

And His words: ﴿Then where are you going?﴾

God, may His remembrance be exalted, says: Then where are you turning away from this Qur'an and deviating from it?

Those who interpret the Qur'an have said the same as what we have said.

Mention of those who said that:

- Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, ﴿Then where are you going?﴾: He says: Then where are you deviating from My Book and My obedience? It has been said: ﴿Then where are you going?﴾ and it was not said: "to where are you going", just as it is said: "I went to Syria" and "I went to the market". And it is related from the Arabs by hearing: "inṭalaqa bihi al-ghawr" (he set off with him to the depression), on the meaning of dropping the preposition; and it is recited for some of the Banu 'Uqayl:

"Hanifa shouts at us when it sees us, / and to which land does it go for the shouting?" [[In the manuscript: "al-malik 'ala al-malik", and they are the same.]]

Meaning: "to which land are you going?" and dropping the preposition in this was deemed permissible due to its common usage.

God, may His remembrance be exalted, says: ﴿Obeyed there﴾ means Gabriel (ﷺ), obeyed in the heavens, whom the angels obey. ﴿Trustworthy﴾ means: trustworthy with God regarding His revelation and His message, and everything else He has entrusted to him.

Those who interpret the Qur'an (ahl al-ta'wil) have said the same as what we have said.

- Bishr narrated to us, saying: Khalid ibn 'Abd Allah al-Wasiti narrated to us, saying: al-Mughira narrated to us, from Ibrahim, ﴿and he is not niggardly regarding the unseen﴾: not stingy.

- Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words, ﴿and he is not niggardly regarding the unseen﴾: He said: Indeed this Qur'an is unseen; God gave it to Muhammad, and he disseminated it, taught it and called to it. - Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, ﴿and he is not niggardly regarding the unseen﴾: He said: stingy.

- Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words, ﴿and he is not niggardly regarding the unseen﴾: The unseen is the Qur'an. None of them was stingy, concealed or spoke conjecturally.

Mention of those who recited it with ẓā' and interpreted it as we have mentioned, from among those who interpret the Qur'an.

- Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, saying: Shu'ba narrated to us, from Abu al-Mu'alla, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that he used to recite this letter ﴿and he is not ẓanīn regarding the unseen﴾. - Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my paternal uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words, ﴿and he is not ẓanīn regarding the unseen﴾: He says: not accused regarding what he has been given, and he is not suspected regarding what he has been given.

- Bishr narrated to us, saying: Khalid ibn 'Abd Allah al-Wasiti narrated to us, saying: al-Mughira narrated to us, from Ibrahim, ﴿and he is not ẓanīn regarding the unseen﴾: He said: accused.

- Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from Sufyan, from 'Asim, from Zirr, ﴿and he is not ẓanīn regarding the unseen﴾: He said: the unseen is the Qur'an. In our recitation, ﴿ẓanīn﴾: accused.

He used to come to him in the form of a man called Dihya. So he came to him on the day he saw him in his form, having filled the whole horizon, wearing green silk brocade, hung with pearls. That is God's words: ﴿And he certainly saw him on the clear horizon﴾. And it is mentioned that this verse, in "When the sun is folded up" (81:1), ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger﴾ refers to Gabriel, up to His words ﴿and he is not niggardly regarding the unseen﴾, which means the Prophet (ﷺ).

* *

And His words: ﴿And he is not niggardly regarding the unseen﴾

The readers differed in their recitation of this. The majority of the readers of Medina and Kufa recited it ﴿bi-ḍanīn﴾ with the letter ḍād, meaning that he is not stingy towards them in teaching them what God taught him and sent down to him of His Book. Some of the Meccan readers, some of the Basran readers and some of the Kufan readers recited it ﴿bi-ẓanīn﴾ with the letter ẓā', meaning that he is not accused regarding what he informs them of from God's tidings.

Mention of those who recited it with ḍād and interpreted it in the way we have described, from among those who interpret the Qur'an: Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from 'Asim, from Zirr, ﴿and he is not ẓanīn regarding the unseen﴾. He said: al-ẓanīn: the accused. In your recitation: ﴿ḍanīn﴾, and ḍanīn: the stingy; and the unseen: the Qur'an.

- Bishr narrated to us, saying: Khalid ibn 'Abd Allah al-Wasiti narrated to us, saying: al-Mughira narrated to us, from Ibrahim, ﴿and he is not niggardly regarding the unseen﴾: not stingy.

- Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words, ﴿and he is not niggardly regarding the unseen﴾: He said: he does not withhold from you what he knows.

- Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words, ﴿and he is not niggardly regarding the unseen﴾: He said: Indeed this Qur'an is unseen; God gave it to Muhammad, and he disseminated it, taught it and called to it. By God, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) did not withhold it.

- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, from 'Asim, from Zirr, ﴿and he is not ẓanīn regarding the unseen﴾: He said: in our recitation, "accused". And whoever recites ﴿ḍanīn﴾ says: "stingy".

- Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, ﴿and he is not niggardly regarding the unseen﴾: He said: stingy.

- Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words, ﴿and he is not niggardly regarding the unseen﴾: The unseen is the Qur'an. He did not withhold it from anyone among mankind; he delivered and conveyed it. God sent it with the Trustworthy Spirit, Gabriel, to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Gabriel conveyed to Muhammad what God had entrusted to him, and Muhammad conveyed to the servants what God and Gabriel had entrusted to him. None of them was stingy, concealed or spoke conjecturally.

- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from 'Ata', from 'Amir, regarding His words, ﴿and he is not niggardly regarding the unseen﴾: meaning the Prophet (ﷺ).

Mention of those who recited it with ẓā' and interpreted it as we have mentioned, from among those who interpret the Qur'an.

- Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: al-Muharibi narrated to us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, that he recited: ﴿bi-ẓanīn﴾ and said: not accused.

- Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, saying: Shu'ba narrated to us, from Abu al-Mu'alla, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that he used to recite this letter ﴿and he is not ẓanīn regarding the unseen﴾. I said to Sa'id ibn Jubayr: What is al-ẓanīn? He said: not accused.

- Ya'qub related to me, saying: Ibn 'Ulayya narrated to us, from Abu al-Mu'alla, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that he recited: ﴿and he is not ẓanīn regarding the unseen﴾. I said: And what is al-ẓanīn? He said: the accused.

- Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my paternal uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words, ﴿and he is not ẓanīn regarding the unseen﴾: He says: not accused regarding what he has been given, and he is not suspected regarding what he has been given.

- Bishr narrated to us, saying: Khalid ibn 'Abd Allah al-Wasiti narrated to us, saying: al-Mughira narrated to us, from Ibrahim, ﴿and he is not ẓanīn regarding the unseen﴾: He said: accused.

- Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from Sufyan, from 'Asim, from Zirr, ﴿and he is not ẓanīn regarding the unseen﴾: He said: the unseen is the Qur'an. In our recitation, ﴿ẓanīn﴾: accused.

- I was told, from al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd narrated to us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His words, ﴿ẓanīn﴾: He said: not accused regarding what God has sent down.

Some of the scholars of Arabic have interpreted it to mean: and he is not weak regarding the unseen, but he is capable of bearing it and able to manage it; and its basis is the Arabs' saying of a weak man: "huwa ẓanūn" (he is weak).

The more correct of the two recitations in my view is that which the copies of the Muslims' codices agree upon, even though their recitations differ concerning it. That is ﴿ḍanīn﴾ with ḍād, because that is how it is written in all of their copies. Since that is so, the more correct of the two interpretations is the interpretation of the one who interpreted it as: Muhammad, regarding what God taught him of His revelation and His sending down, is not stingy in teaching it to you, O people, but rather he is eager that you believe in it and learn it.

* *

And His words: ﴿And it is not the word of an accursed devil﴾

God, may His remembrance be exalted, says: This Qur'an is not the word of a cursed, expelled devil, but rather it is the speech and revelation of God.

* *

And His words: ﴿Then where are you going?﴾

God, may His remembrance be exalted, says: Then where are you turning away from this Qur'an and deviating from it?

Those who interpret the Qur'an have said the same as what we have said.

Mention of those who said that:

- Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, ﴿Then where are you going?﴾: He says: Then where are you deviating from My Book and My obedience? It has been said: ﴿Then where are you going?﴾ and it was not said: "to where are you going", just as it is said: "I went to Syria" and "I went to the market". And it is related from the Arabs by hearing: "inṭalaqa bihi al-ghawr" (he set off with him to the depression), on the meaning of dropping the preposition; and it is recited for some of the Banu 'Uqayl:

"Hanifa shouts at us when it sees us, / and to which land does it go for the shouting?" [[In the manuscript: "al-malik 'ala al-malik", and they are the same.]]

Meaning: "to which land are you going?" and dropping the preposition in this was deemed permissible due to its common usage.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 81, verses 27–29:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is nothing but a reminder to the worlds (27) for whoever of you wills to take a straight path (28). And you do not will except that Allah wills, Lord of the worlds (29).﴾

His saying, may His remembrance be exalted: ﴿It﴾ means this Qur'an, and His saying ﴿it is﴾ refers to the mention of the Qur'an. ﴿Nothing but a reminder to the worlds﴾ means nothing but an admonition and an exhortation to the worlds, of jinn and mankind. ﴿For whoever of you wills to take a straight path﴾: by this, He, may His remembrance be exalted, made it a reminder only for those among the worlds who wish to go straight, and did not make it a reminder for all of them. So the lam in His saying ﴿for whoever of you wills﴾ is a substitution (badal) for the lam in ﴿to the worlds﴾. The meaning of the statement is: It is nothing but a reminder for whoever of you wills to go straight on the path of truth, so that he follows it and believes in it.

The interpreters (ahl al-ta'wil) have said something similar to what we have said regarding this.

Mention of those who said that:

Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us. And al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿for whoever of you wills to take a straight path﴾, he said: he follows the truth.

* *

As for His saying: ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills, Lord of the worlds﴾

His saying, may His remembrance be exalted: And you do not will, O people, to be upright upon the truth, except that Allah wills that.

It is mentioned that the cause for which this verse was revealed was:

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Sa'id ibn Abd al-Aziz, from Sulayman ibn Musa: When ﴿for whoever of you wills to take a straight path﴾ was revealed, Abu Jahl said: That is up to us; if we wish, we go straight. So it was revealed: ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills, Lord of the worlds﴾.

Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Sa'id ibn Abd al-Aziz, from Sulayman ibn Musa, who said: When this verse ﴿for whoever of you wills to take a straight path﴾ was revealed, Abu Jahl said: The matter is up to us; if we wish we go straight, and if we wish we do not go straight. So Allah revealed: ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills, Lord of the worlds﴾.

Ibn al-Barqi narrated to me, saying: Amr ibn Abi Salamah narrated to us, from Sa'id, from Sulayman ibn Musa, who said: When this verse was revealed: ﴿for whoever of you wills to take a straight path﴾, Abu Jahl said: That is up to us; if we wish we go straight, and if we wish we do not go straight. So Allah revealed: ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills, Lord of the worlds﴾.

End of the commentary on Surah ﴿When the sun is wrapped up﴾.
